details:
**Killing Laius at the crossroads**
Oedipus unknowingly kills his real father, King Laius of Thebes (son of Labdacus), at a place where three roads meet in Phocis, where the roads to Delphi, Daulis, and Thebes join. They quarrel over the right of way, Laius strikes him with a goad or scepter, and Oedipus kills him and all but one of his servants. The survivor later claims a band of robbers did it.

**Jocasta**
The queen of Thebes, Laius's widow, and Oedipus's mother, whom he marries without knowing who she is. They have four children: Eteocles, Polynices, Antigone, and Ismene. When the truth comes out in Oedipus Rex, she hangs herself.

**Blinding himself with Jocasta's pins**
After finding Jocasta's body, Oedipus pulls the gold pins (brooches) from her dress and stabs out his own eyes, so he will not have to look upon what he has done.

**The riddle of the Sphinx**
The Sphinx terrorizes Thebes by asking travelers what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening. Oedipus answers "man" (a baby crawls, an adult walks, and an old man uses a cane), and the Sphinx kills herself. As a reward he becomes king of Thebes and marries the widowed queen.

**Mount Cithaeron and the pierced ankles**
Because an oracle warned that his son would kill him, Laius has the infant Oedipus's ankles pierced and bound together and orders him left to die on Mount Cithaeron. The servant gives him to a shepherd instead. The name Oedipus means "swollen foot," after this injury.

**Polybus and Merope**
The childless king and queen of Corinth (the queen is called Periboea in some sources) who raise Oedipus as their own son. When he hears an oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, he flees Corinth to avoid them, which leads him straight to Thebes.

**Oedipus Rex (Oedipus Tyrannus)**
Sophocles's tragedy, also called Oedipus the King. It opens with Thebans placing olive branches wrapped in wool on an altar, begging Oedipus to end a plague, and Creon returns from Delphi with word that Laius's killer must be found. Oedipus vows to find the murderer and slowly discovers it is himself.

**Tiresias**
The blind prophet of Thebes. Oedipus summons him for help finding Laius's killer, and when Tiresias reluctantly tells him "you yourself are the criminal you seek," Oedipus angrily accuses him and Creon of plotting against him and mocks his blindness. Tiresias laments that "wisdom is a dreadful thing when it brings no profit to its possessor."

**The messenger from Corinth and the shepherd**
A messenger arrives to report that Polybus has died and that Corinth wants Oedipus as king. Trying to ease Oedipus's fear, he reveals that Polybus and Merope were not his real parents, since he himself, as a shepherd on Cithaeron, received the baby from one of Laius's servants. Oedipus then threatens that old herdsman with torture until he confirms the truth.

**Oedipus at Colonus**
Sophocles's last play. The blind, exiled Oedipus, guided by Antigone, arrives at Colonus near Athens and takes refuge in a grove sacred to the Furies (Eumenides). Prophecy says the land where he is buried will be blessed, so Theseus protects him from Creon. After three peals of thunder, Oedipus goes off to die in a secret place that only Theseus may see.

**Cursing Eteocles and Polynices**
Oedipus curses his sons to kill each other, in Oedipus at Colonus because they did not help him in exile, and in the epic Thebaid because they served him at the silver table and with the golden cup of his ancestor Cadmus, against his wishes. The brothers agree to rule Thebes in alternate years, then kill each other in single combat during the war of the Seven Against Thebes (dramatized by Aeschylus).

**Antigone and Ismene**
Oedipus's daughters by Jocasta, so they are also his half-sisters. At the end of Oedipus Rex he asks Creon to care for them, and Antigone guides her blind father into exile. Her later decision to bury Polynices against Creon's decree, which gets her sealed in a tomb where she hangs herself, is the subject of Sophocles's Antigone.

**"Count no mortal happy"**
The closing lesson of Oedipus Rex: no one should be called happy until he has died free of suffering. E. R. Dodds's famous essay "On Misunderstanding the Oedipus Rex" argues against reading the play as simply about fate or a tragic flaw.

**Early epic versions: Hesiod and the Oedipodea**
In Works and Days Hesiod says some of the generation of heroes died fighting at seven-gated Thebes for the flocks of Oedipus. In the lost epic Oedipodea, attributed to Cinaethon of Sparta, Oedipus's children are born to a second wife, Euryganeia, rather than to Jocasta.

**Later adaptations: Dryden and Velikovsky**
John Dryden and Nathaniel Lee wrote an English Oedipus that adds a new character, Adrastus. The fringe writer Immanuel Velikovsky's book Oedipus and Akhnaton argues that the Oedipus myth was based on the Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten.
